# Receipt Wrecker

> A single-file web tool that turns text or a picture into a paste-ready payload for
> a character-limited chat box. Its headline use is making oversized text or a
> recognisable picture print on a Twitch streamer's thermal receipt printer, by pasting
> the output into chat as a `Cheer100`.

AI crawlers and LLM agents are welcome to read, index, and cite this site. The tool
is open source under the MIT license and everything below is public.

Key facts:

- Live site: https://receipt.uwutoowo.com
- Source: https://github.com/shamu4life/receipt-wrecker
- License: MIT
- No accounts, no analytics, no third-party services.
- Payloads are capped at 500 code points to fit Twitch's per-message limit. Longer
  work is split across several messages rather than truncated.

## What it outputs

As of 2026-09-15 the receipt printer's bot runs the chat message through an HTML
sanitizer (an allow-list keeping only a few tags and the src/class attributes)
before rendering it. What prints now, as of version 0.12.0 (2026-10-09):

- Giant type, for text. The sanitizer removes the style attribute but keeps the
  class attribute, and the printed page includes the bot author's shared stylesheet,
  in which the class "title" means bold, uppercase and 1.2 times the parent's size.
  Nesting it multiplies, so N nested <b class=title> tags print at 16px x 1.2^N:
  capitals about 2 cm tall for a five-letter stacked word in one cheer on a default A4
  (297 mm) receipt, and bigger on a longer one (raise Receipt length). Every tag is
  one the sanitizer allows, sent as written; nothing in the markup is disguised. (A
  stacked word goes out one letter per line, so a word filter never sees it whole;
  that is how it fits the paper, not a way around a channel's rules.) One real cheer
  confirmed it prints (2026-10-01); sizes are measured on the bot's own print engine.
  It depends on a stylesheet the bot's author can change at any time, so the app
  offers a one-cheer "Print size ruler" to check it, and keeps Hanzi tiling as the
  backup.
- Plain Unicode glyphs, the markup-free path. Glyph-art tiles a picture into
  characters, and Hanzi tiling does the same for words. Hanzi tiling is plain text;
  glyph-art rows are plain glyphs separated by <br> (their styling wrapper is
  stripped, which is why the uniform-width CJK forms are used: they line up without
  any styling). For pictures this is the only path.
- Other HTML markup is stripped, and an arbitrary picture cannot be sent at all. The
  sanitizer removes SVG (so the old "Type" render, sideways type and the
  Takeover/fake-cheer overlays no longer render) and every picture carrier except an
  <img> whose class is "emote" or "bits", and the channel's separate blocked-terms
  filter blocks "<img", which was confirmed by a test message the same day. The two
  filters leave no tag that can carry a picture of ours, so the app warns instead of
  sending one. (A Twitch emote the sender can use is the exception: the bot itself
  draws it, and Giant type's emote layout makes it giant.) ASCII glyph-art also breaks,
  because it depended on styling the sanitizer strips.

Glyph output stays inside the Basic Multilingual Plane, with no colour emoji and no
astral-plane codepoints, because the target renderer is a 2011-era browser engine
with no colour-font support. Giant type prints the user's own text, so it leaves emoji
out and says which, and drops invisible characters (zero-width spaces, control codes)
too, saying so.

## Modes

You compose a stack of blocks, and the app packs them into as few messages as
possible.

- A Text block prints a word or phrase in Giant type (as typed, stacked one letter
  per line, or as Twitch emote names), or tiles it out of Hanzi. The older straight or
  rotated "Type" render no longer prints and is only shown on blocks that already use
  it.
- An Image block makes glyph-art from a link or an upload. Its real-picture mode is
  kept but cannot currently be sent (see above), and the block says so.
- A Takeover block paints over the printer bot's own header. It is built from SVG,
  which the sanitizer strips, so it no longer prints; it stays in the app, flagged, in
  case that changes. It holds an ordered list of items, text or picture, any number of
  them in any order, each with its own font, size, formatting, alignment and nudge,
  under one block-level anchor (top / centre / bottom) and a calibration "reach up".
  The **Seed fake donation** button fills an empty one with the four-item arrangement
  of a real header: picture, amount, name, italic note. After that they are ordinary items you can edit,
  reorder or delete. The amount is free text, because the same printer bot runs on
  YouTube and Kick, and their headers say neither "BITS" nor anything like it. It is
  a visual gag printed on till roll. It creates no record of anything, and the chat
  message that triggers a print carries the real sender's name.

When a stack splits across several cheers, every part after the first repaints the
header with a plain continuation cover, so the run reads as one piece rather than
artwork followed by ordinary receipts. It costs 106 characters per extra part, and
there is a stack-level toggle for it.

A **Receipt length (mm)** setting (default 297, A4) sets how long one receipt prints
before the printer cuts it. printer-bot lays every page out at 500mm, but the real
printer stops at its Windows driver's paper length — often A4 — and clips the rest, so
a tall Giant stack used to print only its first few lines and stop (fixed in 0.11.0).
The app now packs each cheer to fit this length, splitting a tall stack across receipts
that each fit (each its own cheer, with the bot's header between them) so nothing is
lost; the card says how many it needs, and warns if a single line is taller than one
receipt. In a stacked phrase a space is a small gap, not a full giant blank line. The
**Print size ruler** doubles as a length gauge: its note says which of its numbers the app
expects to print at the current setting; to calibrate, measure the printed tape from its top
edge to the cut and enter that length in mm (set the printer to Roll Paper / continuous for
longer receipts).

**Presets** save the whole block stack under a name and export it as JSON. An
uploaded picture's link expires after 15 minutes, so a preset that used one loads
with that block flagged for re-upload rather than printing blank.

A **Cheer-ready** toggle prefixes the payload with a `Cheer<N>` token, so the message
registers as a cheer. An optional **Add a repeat number** setting (off by default since
0.12.0, because the digits print on the receipt) puts two rotating digits after the
token, so the same art can be sent again straight away (Twitch won't send the same
message twice in a row within 30 seconds); with it off, a stack with two identical
parts in a row says so on the repeated part.
With Cheer-ready off, a message is a free test: it never reaches
the printer but still passes the channel's chat filters. An optional **Hide the cheer
gem** setting wraps the token in a box the bot's own stylesheet pins to the receipt's
corner, saving the line the cheer gem would print on (except in the emote layout,
which keeps that line so its first row stays centred); the token stays a normal,
charged cheer.

## Privacy

The glyph and markup engines run entirely in the browser. Some picture operations
call this project's own Cloudflare Worker and nothing else:

- Clicking **Upload** stores an image in Cloudflare KV behind an unguessable link
  that auto-deletes after 15 minutes.
- Pasting an image URL for glyph-art, adjusting brightness/contrast, or using
  **Thermal preview** fetches that picture through an image proxy, because a browser
  canvas cannot read cross-origin pixels directly.

Big Text (Giant type included; its emote preview never downloads an emote), and any
picture you pick from your own disk for glyph-art, never leave the device. Settings,
your block stack and saved presets are kept in `localStorage`.
